newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore says not policing Internet users.
newsitem.headline: Singapore says not policing Internet users.

text.p: Singapore is not policing the Internet and users who visit pornographic sites need not fear prosecution, the chief executive officer of the Singapore Broadcasting Authority (SBA) said on Tuesday.
Goh Liang Kwang was responding to Reuters' enquiries following the conviction last month of a Singaporean man for downloading sex films from the Internet.
Lai Chee Chuan, 41, was fined a total of Singapore $61,000 (US$43,000) for copying 61 obscene films from the international computer network, the first such case in Singapore.

Lai's prosecution was connected to an Interpol operation over an international child pornography ring, not "as a result of any blanket policing of the system for the purpose of netting individuals accessing the Internet", Goh said in a statement.
"I would like to assure Netters that we do not interfere with what individuals access on the Internet in the privacy of their homes," Goh said.
"We do not track, nor do we monitor individuals' access, and neither do the ISPs (Internet Service Providers).
"Individuals who accidentally stumble upon pornographic sites need not fear about any action from the (SBA). The mere act of visiting is not an offence."
Singapore bans pornographic magazines, including such "soft" publications as "Playboy" and "Penthouse".
Worries over possible Internet censorship surfaced last month after the SBA told its licenced service providers to install by September 15 systems capable of blocking "undesireable" Internet sites.
All three of Singapore's providers installed special "proxy" computers which act as relay stations between their domestic consumers and the Internet outside Singapore.
But Goh said the SBA had only asked the providers to block a few dozen high-profile sites, "all of them pornography".
